title: Git and the Command Line
description: Use the shell and Git the way senior engineers do: from pipes and permissions to rebasing, recovering lost work and understanding what Git stores under the hood.

chapters.title: Shell Basics: Navigation, Pipes and Text Search
chapters.summary: Move around the filesystem, combine small commands with pipes and redirection, and find files and text fast with find and grep.

lesson.heading: The shell, the prompt and paths
lesson.body:
A shell (bash, zsh, fish, PowerShell) reads a command line, expands it, and starts programs. On macOS the default is zsh; most Linux servers and CI runners use bash. Commands follow the shape `command -flags arguments`.

Every process has a **current working directory**. Paths starting with `/` are absolute; everything else is relative to the current directory. `.` is the current directory, `..` is the parent and `~` expands to your home directory.

- `pwd` prints the working directory
- `ls -la` lists all files, including hidden dotfiles, with permissions and sizes
- `cd -` jumps back to the previous directory
- `mkdir -p a/b/c` creates nested directories without failing if they exist
- `rm -rf dir` deletes recursively with no confirmation and no trash can, so double-check the path

code.source:
pwd                     # /home/ana/projects
cd ~/projects/api       # absolute via home
cd ../web               # sibling directory
ls -la                  # long listing incl. dotfiles
mkdir -p src/utils      # create nested dirs
cp -r src backup        # copy a directory
mv old.txt new.txt      # rename or move
cat package.json        # print a file
less server.log         # page through a big file (q to quit)

lesson.heading: Streams, redirection and pipes
lesson.body:
Every process gets three standard streams: stdin (0), stdout (1) and stderr (2). Redirection connects them to files; pipes connect one program's stdout to the next program's stdin. This is the Unix philosophy: small tools that each do one thing, combined with `|`.

- `>` writes stdout to a file, truncating it; `>>` appends
- `2>` redirects stderr; `2>&1` sends stderr wherever stdout currently goes
- `<` feeds a file to stdin
- `|` pipes stdout only, so errors still print to the terminal unless you redirect them
- `/dev/null` discards anything written to it

Order matters: `cmd > out.log 2>&1` captures both streams, but `cmd 2>&1 > out.log` sends stderr to the terminal because stderr was duplicated before stdout moved.

code.source:
npm test > test.log 2>&1        # both streams to a file
npm run build 2> errors.txt      # only errors
curl -s https://api.example.com/users | jq '.[0].name'
cat access.log | grep ' 500 ' | wc -l     # count 500 responses
history | grep docker | tail -5
sort names.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn | head  # most frequent lines

lesson.heading: Searching text with grep
lesson.body:
`grep` prints lines matching a pattern. It is the fastest way to answer questions like "where is this function used?" or "which log lines mention this user?". Many developers use `rg` (ripgrep), which is faster and respects `.gitignore` by default, but grep is installed everywhere, including minimal Docker images.

- `-r` recursive, `-n` line numbers, `-i` case-insensitive
- `-l` print only file names, `-c` count matches
- `-v` invert (lines that do NOT match)
- `-E` extended regex (`|`, `+`, `?` without backslashes)
- `-w` match whole words, `--include='*.ts'` restrict to file patterns
- `-A 3`, `-B 3`, `-C 3` show lines after, before or around each match

Quote patterns with single quotes so the shell does not expand `*`, `$` or spaces before grep sees them.

code.source:
grep -rn 'useEffect' src/                 # every usage with line numbers
grep -rl --include='*.ts' 'TODO' .         # files containing TODO
grep -E 'ERROR|FATAL' app.log | grep -v healthcheck
grep -C 2 'NullPointer' server.log        # 2 lines of context
rg 'fetchUser\(' -t ts                    # ripgrep equivalent

lesson.heading: Finding files with find and acting on them
lesson.body:
`find` walks a directory tree and filters by name, type, size, modification time and more. Its first argument is where to start; expressions follow.

- `-name '*.log'` matches the file name (case-sensitive), `-iname` ignores case
- `-type f` files, `-type d` directories
- `-mtime -1` modified in the last 24 hours, `-size +10M` bigger than 10 MB
- `-not -path '*/node_modules/*'` excludes paths
- `-delete` or `-exec cmd {} +` act on results

`xargs` turns stdin lines into arguments for another command. Use `find ... -print0 | xargs -0` so file names with spaces do not break into separate arguments.

code.source:
find . -name '*.test.ts' -not -path '*/node_modules/*'
find /var/log -type f -size +100M          # big log files
find . -name '*.tmp' -mtime +7 -delete      # delete week-old temp files
find src -name '*.js' -exec wc -l {} +      # line counts
find . -name '*.png' -print0 | xargs -0 du -h | sort -h | tail

lesson.heading: Globs, quoting and command chaining
lesson.body:
The shell expands globs before the program runs: `*.js` becomes a list of matching names. If nothing matches, bash passes the literal `*.js` while zsh errors by default. Quoting controls expansion:

- Single quotes `'...'` are literal: no variables, no globs
- Double quotes `"..."` expand `$VAR` and `$(cmd)` but keep spaces together, so always quote variables: `rm "$file"`
- Backslash escapes one character

Chaining operators decide what runs next based on the exit code (0 means success):

- `a && b` runs b only if a succeeded
- `a || b` runs b only if a failed
- `a ; b` runs b regardless
- `$(cmd)` substitutes a command's output into another command

code.source:
npm ci && npm test && npm run build    # stop at first failure
mkdir logs 2>/dev/null || echo 'already exists'
echo "Branch: $(git branch --show-current)"
for f in *.md; do echo "$f"; done
echo $?                                # exit code of last command

keyPoints: Every process has stdin (0), stdout (1) and stderr (2); pipes connect stdout to the next command's stdin.
`>` truncates, `>>` appends, and `cmd > file 2>&1` captures both output streams in one file.
grep searches content (-r, -n, -i, -l, -v, -E); find searches the file tree by name, type, size and time.
Use `-print0 | xargs -0` or `-exec ... {} +` so file names with spaces are handled safely.
Single quotes are literal, double quotes expand variables; always quote variables that hold paths.
`&&` continues only on success (exit code 0), `||` runs on failure.
`rm -rf` has no undo; check paths and variables before running it.

questions.prompt: Which command writes both stdout and stderr of `npm test` into test.log?
questions.explanation: Redirections are processed left to right. `> test.log` first points stdout at the file, then `2>&1` duplicates stderr to where stdout now points. In the reversed order, stderr is duplicated to the terminal before stdout moves.

questions.prompt: You want only the names of TypeScript files under src/ that contain the string `fetchUser`. Which command fits?
questions.explanation: `-r` recurses, `-l` prints only file names and `--include` limits the search to .ts files. `find -name` matches file names, not content, and `-v` inverts the match.

questions.prompt: What does `cat access.log | grep ' 500 ' | wc -l` output?
options: The number of words in access.log
questions.explanation: grep filters matching lines and `wc -l` counts the lines it receives on stdin, so the result is a count of matching lines.

questions.prompt: What happens with `npm ci && npm test` if `npm ci` exits with code 1?
options: npm test runs with a warning
questions.explanation: `&&` runs the right-hand command only when the left one exits with 0. A non-zero exit code short-circuits the chain, which is why CI scripts chain steps with &&.

questions.prompt: Why is `find . -name '*.png' -print0 | xargs -0 rm` safer than `find . -name '*.png' | xargs rm`?
options: It handles file names containing spaces or newlines correctly
It asks for confirmation before deleting
questions.explanation: By default xargs splits input on whitespace, so `my photo.png` becomes two arguments. `-print0` separates names with a NUL byte and `xargs -0` splits only on NUL, which cannot appear in file names.

questions.prompt: Given `name=world`, what does `echo '$name'` print?
questions.explanation: Single quotes disable all expansion, so the literal text `$name` is printed. Double quotes (`"$name"`) would print `world`.

questions.prompt: A pipe (`|`) passes both stdout and stderr of the left command to the right command.
questions.explanation: A plain pipe only connects stdout. Error output still goes to the terminal unless you add `2>&1` before the pipe (or use `|&` in bash).

questions.prompt: In bash, an exit code of 0 means the command succeeded.
questions.explanation: By convention 0 is success and any non-zero value (1-255) signals an error. `$?` holds the exit code of the last command, and `&&`/`||` branch on it.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which grep flags are matched correctly with their meaning?
options: -l: print only names of matching files
questions.explanation: -v inverts the match (prints non-matching lines), and -c prints a count of matching lines. Color is controlled by --color.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the operator ___ appends output to a file instead of overwriting it.
questions.explanation: `>` truncates the target file first, while `>>` opens it in append mode, which is what you want for log files.

questions.prompt: A production log is 5 GB. How would you find the 10 most frequent error messages from the command line?
questions.answer:
- Avoid opening it in an editor; stream it with tools that read line by line.
- Filter first: `grep 'ERROR' app.log` so later steps process less data.
- Normalize the message, for example cut off timestamps with `cut -d' ' -f4-` or `sed` to strip IDs, so identical errors group together.
- Count and rank: `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10`. `uniq -c` only counts adjacent duplicates, which is why the first sort is required.
- Full pipeline: `grep ERROR app.log | cut -d' ' -f4- | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10`.
- If the log is compressed, use `zgrep` or `zcat file.gz | ...`; for live logs, `tail -f app.log | grep ERROR`.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between stdout and stderr and why programs keep them separate.
questions.answer: stdout (file descriptor 1) carries a program's normal output, stderr (file descriptor 2) carries diagnostics and errors. Keeping them separate lets you pipe or save the real data while errors still reach the person at the terminal, for example `curl url > data.json` still shows connection errors on screen. It also lets tools treat them differently: CI systems often highlight stderr, and you can send errors to a separate file with `2> errors.log`. When you want everything in one place you merge them with `2>&1`. A well-behaved CLI writes machine-readable output to stdout, human messages to stderr, and signals failure with a non-zero exit code.

questions.prompt: How would you find and delete all `.tmp` files older than 7 days under a directory, safely?
questions.answer: First run the search without deleting, to see what would be affected: `find /data -type f -name '*.tmp' -mtime +7`. `-type f` keeps directories out, `-name` is quoted so the shell does not expand the glob, and `-mtime +7` means modified more than 7 days ago. Once the list looks right, add `-delete` (or `-exec rm {} +`). I would avoid `find | xargs rm` without `-print0`/`-0` because file names with spaces split into wrong arguments. For a scheduled cleanup I would put this in a cron job or systemd timer and log the count of deleted files.

chapters.title: Git Basics: The Three Areas and Everyday Commands
chapters.summary: Understand the working tree, staging area and repository, and use status, add, commit, diff, log, restore and .gitignore with confidence.

lesson.heading: Snapshots, not diffs
lesson.body:
Git is a distributed version control system. Every clone holds the full history, so most commands (log, diff, commit, branch) run locally without a network.

A commit is a **snapshot** of the whole project at a point in time, plus metadata: author, committer, timestamp, message and a pointer to its parent commit(s). Git computes diffs on demand by comparing snapshots. Unchanged files are not copied; the new snapshot points at the same stored content.

Each commit is identified by a hash of its content (SHA-1 by default, SHA-256 supported in newer repositories). Change anything, even one character in the message, and you get a different hash. That is why rewriting history changes commit IDs.

code.source:
git config --global user.name "Ana Lima"
git config --global user.email "ana@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

git init my-app        # new repository
git clone https://github.com/org/repo.git   # copy an existing one

lesson.heading: Working tree, index and repository
lesson.body:
Git has three areas, and most confusion disappears once you track which one a command touches:

- **Working tree**: the files on disk that you edit
- **Index (staging area)**: the proposed next commit; `git add` copies the current content of a file here
- **Repository**: the committed history stored in `.git`

`git add` stages a snapshot of the file at that moment. If you edit the file again after adding, `git status` shows it as both staged and modified, and the commit will contain the staged version, not your latest edit.

Staging lets you build focused commits from a messy working tree. `git add -p` walks through each hunk and asks whether to stage it.

code.source:
git status                 # what changed, what is staged
git add src/api.ts         # stage one file
git add -p                 # stage hunk by hunk
git commit -m "Add retry to user API client"
git commit -am "Fix typo"  # stage tracked files + commit (skips new files)

lesson.heading: Seeing changes: diff and log
lesson.body:
`git diff` has three common forms, matching the three areas:

- `git diff` working tree vs index (unstaged changes)
- `git diff --staged` (alias `--cached`) index vs last commit (what you are about to commit)
- `git diff main..feature` or `git diff HEAD~3` between commits

`git log` shows history. Useful options: `--oneline`, `--graph --all` for a branch picture, `-p` to include patches, `--author`, `--since=2.weeks`, `-- path` to restrict to a file, and `-S 'text'` (the pickaxe) to find commits that added or removed a string.

`git show <commit>` prints one commit with its diff. `HEAD` is the commit you have checked out; `HEAD~1` is its parent and `HEAD~3` three generations back.

code.source:
git diff                   # unstaged
git diff --staged          # staged, about to be committed
git log --oneline --graph --all -20
git log -p -- src/auth.ts  # history of one file with patches
git log -S 'API_KEY'       # commits that added/removed API_KEY
git show HEAD~1

lesson.heading: Undoing local changes with restore
lesson.body:
Since Git 2.23, `git restore` and `git switch` split the overloaded `git checkout` into clearer commands.

- `git restore file` discards unstaged changes in the working tree (destructive, the edits are gone)
- `git restore --staged file` unstages, keeping your edits in the working tree
- `git restore --source=HEAD~2 file` brings back an older version of a file
- `git commit --amend` replaces the last commit with a new one (new hash); only do this before pushing or on your own branch

`git rm --cached file` stops tracking a file without deleting it from disk, which is how you fix a committed `.env` or `node_modules` (and then add it to `.gitignore`). If a secret was pushed, removing it in a new commit is not enough: it is still in history, so rotate the secret.

code.source:
git restore src/app.ts            # throw away edits
git restore --staged src/app.ts   # unstage, keep edits
git rm --cached .env              # stop tracking, keep file
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
git commit --amend --no-edit      # add staged changes to last commit

lesson.heading: .gitignore and what not to commit
lesson.body:
`.gitignore` lists patterns of untracked files Git should ignore. It does not affect files that are already tracked; untrack them first with `git rm --cached`.

- `node_modules/` a trailing slash matches only directories
- `*.log` any file ending in .log, in any directory
- `/build` a leading slash anchors to the directory of the .gitignore
- `!keep.log` negates an earlier pattern
- `**/temp` matches temp at any depth

Typical ignores: dependencies, build output, coverage reports, `.env*` files with secrets, editor folders and OS files like `.DS_Store`. Commit lockfiles (`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`) so every machine installs the same versions. `git check-ignore -v path` tells you which rule ignores a file.

code.source:
# dependencies and build output
node_modules/
dist/
.next/
coverage/

# secrets
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

# noise
*.log
.DS_Store

keyPoints: A commit is a full snapshot plus metadata and parent pointer(s), identified by a content hash.
Three areas: working tree (your files), index (next commit), repository (history in .git).
`git diff` shows unstaged changes; `git diff --staged` shows what will be committed.
`git restore file` discards edits; `git restore --staged file` only unstages.
Amending or rewriting a commit creates a new hash, so avoid it on shared history.
.gitignore only affects untracked files; use `git rm --cached` to stop tracking a committed file.
Commit lockfiles; never commit secrets, and rotate any secret that reached a remote.

questions.prompt: You edited `app.ts`, ran `git add app.ts`, then edited it again. What does `git commit` (without -a) include?
options: Only the first edit (the version staged by git add)
Nothing, because the file has unstaged changes
questions.explanation: `git add` copies the file's content into the index at that moment. The commit is built from the index, so the later edit stays in the working tree until you add it again.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the changes that are staged and will go into the next commit?
questions.explanation: `git diff` compares the working tree to the index (unstaged changes). `git diff --staged` (or `--cached`) compares the index to HEAD, which is exactly the next commit's change.

questions.prompt: You accidentally committed `.env` two commits ago and have not pushed. Adding `.env` to .gitignore now will:
options: Stop Git from tracking it immediately
Do nothing for the already tracked file
questions.explanation: .gitignore only applies to untracked files. You must run `git rm --cached .env` to stop tracking it, and rewrite the two commits (for example with interactive rebase) if it must not exist in history.

questions.prompt: Which command unstages `config.ts` while keeping your edits in the working tree?
questions.explanation: `--staged` restores the index entry from HEAD, leaving the working tree alone. Plain `git restore` overwrites the working tree copy and loses your edits.

questions.prompt: Which `git log` option finds commits that added or removed the string `featureFlagX`?
questions.explanation: `-S` (the pickaxe) finds commits where the number of occurrences of the string changed. `--grep` searches commit messages, not code.

questions.prompt: What does `HEAD~2` refer to?
options: The grandparent of the current commit
questions.explanation: `~n` walks back n generations following first parents. `HEAD~1` is the parent and `HEAD~2` the grandparent.

questions.prompt: Git stores each commit as a list of line diffs against the previous commit.
questions.explanation: Git's model is snapshots: each commit points to a tree describing the full project. Identical files are shared by hash. Packfiles use delta compression internally for storage, but that is an optimization, not the data model.

questions.prompt: `git commit --amend` changes the hash of the last commit.
questions.explanation: Amending creates a brand new commit object with different content or metadata, so it gets a new hash. Anyone who already pulled the old commit now has diverging history.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which files should normally be committed in a Node.js project?
options: dist/ build output (for a deployed web app)
questions.explanation: Lockfiles make installs reproducible and .env.example documents required variables. node_modules and build output are generated, and real secrets must never be committed.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: `git ___ -p` lets you stage changes hunk by hunk.
questions.explanation: `git add -p` (patch mode) shows each change hunk and asks y/n/s(plit)/e(dit), so you can split unrelated edits into separate commits.

questions.prompt: Explain the staging area. Why does Git have it when other VCSs commit directly?
questions.answer: The staging area (index) is the draft of the next commit. `git add` copies file content into it and `git commit` turns it into a snapshot. It exists so you can shape commits deliberately: if you fixed a bug and also refactored something unrelated, you stage and commit them separately, even hunk by hunk with `git add -p`. That produces small, reviewable, revertable commits and makes tools like bisect more useful. It also lets you review exactly what you are committing with `git diff --staged`. The index also caches file metadata, which is why `git status` is fast on large repos.

questions.prompt: A teammate pushed an AWS key to the main branch an hour ago. What do you do?
questions.answer:
- Treat the key as compromised immediately: revoke or rotate it in AWS first, because bots scan public repos within minutes and even private repos are cloned to many machines.
- Check CloudTrail or billing for misuse during the exposure window.
- Remove the secret from the code and load it from an environment variable or a secrets manager.
- Decide whether to purge history with `git filter-repo` or BFG. That requires a force push and every clone re-syncing, so it is coordinated, but it matters less than rotation because the old key is already dead.
- Prevent recurrence: add the file to .gitignore, enable secret scanning and push protection (GitHub), and add a pre-commit hook like gitleaks.

questions.prompt: What makes a good commit and a good commit message?
questions.answer: A good commit is atomic: one logical change that builds and passes tests on its own, so it can be reviewed, reverted or cherry-picked independently. Formatting changes and behavior changes go in separate commits. The message has a short imperative subject line around 50 characters ("Add retry to payment client"), a blank line, then a body explaining why the change was made and any trade-offs, since the diff already shows what changed. Reference the ticket or issue. Many teams also use Conventional Commits prefixes like `feat:` or `fix:` so changelogs and version bumps can be generated automatically.

chapters.title: Branches and Remotes
chapters.summary: Create and switch branches, understand what a branch really is, and sync with remotes using fetch, pull and push.

lesson.heading: A branch is just a movable pointer
lesson.body:
A branch is a tiny file containing a commit hash. When you commit on a branch, Git writes the new commit and moves the branch pointer to it. Creating a branch is instant and costs a few bytes, which is why Git encourages short-lived feature branches.

`HEAD` tells Git which branch you are on. Normally HEAD points to a branch name (for example `ref: refs/heads/main`), and that branch points to a commit. If you check out a commit directly, HEAD points straight at the commit: this is **detached HEAD**. New commits made there belong to no branch and become hard to find once you switch away, so create a branch with `git switch -c name` if you want to keep them.

code.source:
git branch                    # list local branches
git switch -c feature/login   # create and switch
git switch main               # switch back
git switch -                  # previous branch
git branch -d feature/login   # delete (refuses if unmerged)
git branch -D feature/login   # force delete
git switch --detach v1.2.0    # look at a tag, detached HEAD

lesson.heading: Remotes and remote-tracking branches
lesson.body:
A remote is a named URL of another copy of the repository; `origin` is the default name given by `git clone`. Git keeps **remote-tracking branches** like `origin/main`: read-only local bookmarks of where the remote's branches were the last time you talked to it.

- `git fetch` downloads new commits and updates `origin/*`, never touching your working tree or local branches
- `git pull` is `git fetch` followed by integrating `origin/<branch>` into the current branch (a merge by default, or a rebase with `--rebase` or `pull.rebase=true`)
- `git push` uploads your commits and moves the remote branch, but only if it is a fast-forward

Your local `main` and `origin/main` are different refs. `git status` compares them and reports "ahead 2, behind 1" using the upstream (tracking) configuration.

code.source:
git remote -v                     # list remotes
git fetch origin                  # update origin/* only
git log --oneline main..origin/main   # commits you don't have yet
git pull --rebase                 # fetch + rebase local commits on top
git push -u origin feature/login  # push and set upstream
git branch -vv                    # show upstream and ahead/behind

lesson.heading: Fast-forward, rejected pushes and force pushing
lesson.body:
A push is accepted if the remote branch's current commit is an ancestor of what you push (a fast-forward). If someone pushed first, your push is rejected with "non-fast-forward": fetch, integrate their commits (merge or rebase), then push again.

`git push --force` overwrites the remote branch with yours, discarding commits you never saw. Prefer `git push --force-with-lease`: it only overwrites if the remote is still where your `origin/<branch>` says it is, so you do not clobber a teammate's push. Protected branches on GitHub or GitLab usually block force pushes to main entirely.

Rule of thumb: rewriting and force pushing your own feature branch is normal; rewriting shared branches is not.

code.source:
git push
# ! [rejected] main -> main (non-fast-forward)
git pull --rebase && git push

# after rebasing your own PR branch
git push --force-with-lease

lesson.heading: Tags and releases
lesson.body:
Tags name specific commits, usually releases. Unlike branches they do not move.

- Lightweight tag: just a name for a commit (`git tag v1.0.0`)
- Annotated tag: a full object with tagger, date, message and optional signature (`git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release 1.0.0"`); use these for releases

Tags are not pushed by default: use `git push origin v1.0.0` or `git push --tags`. Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) is the common naming scheme: bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backwards-compatible features and PATCH for fixes.

code.source:
git tag -a v2.3.0 -m "Release 2.3.0"
git push origin v2.3.0
git tag --list 'v2.*'
git describe --tags      # e.g. v2.3.0-4-g1a2b3c4 (4 commits after tag)

lesson.heading: Keeping a feature branch up to date
lesson.body:
While you work, main moves on. Integrate it regularly so conflicts stay small:

- `git fetch` then `git rebase origin/main` replays your commits on top of the latest main and keeps history linear
- or `git merge origin/main` brings main into your branch with a merge commit, which never rewrites history

Either is fine on a personal branch; team convention decides. Short-lived branches (a day or two) avoid most pain. `git stash` temporarily shelves uncommitted work when you need to switch branches quickly: `git stash push -m "wip"`, then `git stash pop` to reapply and drop it.

code.source:
git stash push -m "wip login form"
git switch main && git pull
git switch feature/login
git rebase main          # or: git merge main
git stash pop
git stash list

keyPoints: A branch is a pointer to a commit; committing moves the current branch forward.
HEAD normally points to a branch; detached HEAD points directly at a commit.
`git fetch` only updates remote-tracking branches like origin/main; `git pull` fetches and then merges or rebases.
Pushes must be fast-forwards unless forced; prefer `--force-with-lease` over `--force`.
Use annotated tags for releases and push them explicitly.
Integrate main into feature branches often and keep branches short-lived.
`git stash` shelves uncommitted changes; `stash pop` reapplies and removes the entry.

questions.prompt: What does `git fetch origin` change?
questions.explanation: fetch downloads objects and updates `origin/*` refs. It never modifies your local branches or files, which makes it always safe to run.

questions.prompt: Your push is rejected as non-fast-forward. What is the usual correct fix on a shared branch?
options: git pull --rebase (or pull) and then push
questions.explanation: Someone else pushed commits you do not have. Integrate them first, then push. Force pushing would delete their work, and reset --hard would delete yours.

questions.prompt: Why is `--force-with-lease` safer than `--force`?
options: It only overwrites the remote if it still matches your last fetched origin/<branch>
It creates a backup branch on the remote
It only works on protected branches
questions.explanation: The lease is the expected remote value. If a teammate pushed since your last fetch, the push fails instead of silently discarding their commits.

questions.prompt: You checked out a commit by hash and made two commits. What state are you in?
questions.explanation: HEAD points directly at a commit rather than a branch. Run `git switch -c new-branch` to keep the commits; otherwise they become reachable only through the reflog.

questions.prompt: By default, `git pull` is equivalent to:
options: git fetch + git merge of the upstream branch
questions.explanation: pull fetches and then integrates the upstream into the current branch. The default integration is merge; `--rebase` or the `pull.rebase` config switches it to rebase.

questions.prompt: Which command lists the commits on origin/main that your local main does not have?
questions.explanation: `A..B` means commits reachable from B but not from A. So `main..origin/main` shows what the remote has that you do not.

questions.prompt: `git push` pushes all of your local tags by default.
questions.explanation: Tags must be pushed explicitly with `git push origin <tag>` or `git push --tags` (or `--follow-tags` for annotated tags reachable from pushed commits).

questions.prompt: Creating a new branch in Git copies all files in the project.
questions.explanation: A branch is a reference file holding one commit hash. Nothing is copied, which is why branching is instant even in huge repositories.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which commands are safe to run at any time without risking local work?
questions.explanation: fetch, status and log only read or update remote-tracking refs. reset --hard discards uncommitted changes and clean -fd deletes untracked files permanently.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: `git push ___ origin feature/x` pushes the branch and sets it as the upstream for future pushes and pulls.
questions.explanation: `-u` (`--set-upstream`) records origin/feature/x as the tracking branch, so plain `git push`, `git pull` and ahead/behind counts work afterwards.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull? Which do you prefer and why?
questions.answer: `git fetch` downloads new commits from the remote and updates remote-tracking refs like origin/main, without changing my branches or files. `git pull` does a fetch and then immediately integrates the upstream into my current branch, by merge by default or rebase if configured. I often fetch first and inspect with `git log main..origin/main` or `git diff`, so I know what is coming before integrating. For day-to-day work I set `pull.rebase=true` (or use `pull --ff-only`) so I do not create noisy "Merge branch main of origin" commits on my local branch. The key point is that fetch is always safe while pull can produce conflicts.

questions.prompt: What is detached HEAD, how do you get into it and how do you get out without losing work?
questions.answer: Detached HEAD means HEAD points directly to a commit instead of to a branch. You get there by checking out a commit hash, a tag or a remote-tracking branch (`git checkout v1.0`, `git switch --detach abc123`), and Git does it during a rebase or bisect. It is fine for looking around or running old code. If you commit there, the commits are not on any branch, so after switching away they are only reachable via the reflog and eventually garbage collected. To keep them, run `git switch -c my-branch` while still detached. If you already left, find the hash with `git reflog` and create a branch at it.

questions.prompt: How do you keep a long-running feature branch in sync with main, and what would you change about the process?
questions.answer: I fetch regularly and either rebase onto origin/main (linear history, but requires a force-with-lease push on my branch) or merge main into the branch (no rewriting, extra merge commits), following the team convention. Doing it daily keeps conflicts small and surfaces integration problems early. But a long-running branch is a smell: I would rather split the work into small PRs that merge to main quickly and hide incomplete features behind a feature flag. That is the core of trunk-based development and avoids the big-bang merge at the end, which is where most painful conflicts and regressions come from.

chapters.title: Merge vs Rebase and Resolving Conflicts
chapters.summary: Know exactly what merge and rebase do to history, when to use each, and how to resolve conflicts calmly.

lesson.heading: What a merge does
lesson.body:
`git merge feature` (run on main) combines histories. Git finds the **merge base** (the best common ancestor), computes what changed on each side since then, and combines the changes.

- **Fast-forward**: if main has no new commits since the branch started, Git just moves the main pointer forward. No merge commit is created.
- **Three-way merge**: if both sides have new commits, Git creates a merge commit with two parents.

`--no-ff` forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible, keeping a visible record that a feature branch existed. `--ff-only` refuses to merge unless it can fast-forward, a safe default for `git pull`.

Merging never rewrites existing commits, so it is always safe on shared branches.

code.source:
git switch main
git merge feature/search          # ff if possible, else merge commit
git merge --no-ff feature/search  # always create a merge commit
git merge --ff-only origin/main   # fail rather than create a merge commit
git merge-base main feature/search  # print the common ancestor

lesson.heading: What a rebase does
lesson.body:
`git rebase main` (run on feature) takes each commit on your branch that is not on main, and replays it one by one on top of main's tip. The result looks as if you started the branch today.

Replayed commits are **new commits** with new hashes, even if their changes are identical. The originals still exist (reachable via the reflog) until garbage collection.

The golden rule: **do not rebase commits that others have based work on**. If you rebase a shared branch and force push, teammates' local copies now contain the old commits, and their next pull duplicates or conflicts. Rebasing your own unpublished or personal PR branch is fine.

code.source:
Before:            A---B---C  feature
                  /
         D---E---F---G  main

git rebase main:
                          A'--B'--C'  feature
                         /
         D---E---F---G  main

git merge feature (on main):
                  A---B---C
                 /         \
         D---E---F---G------M  main

lesson.heading: Choosing between merge, rebase and squash
lesson.body:
All three end up with the same code; they differ in history shape.

- **Merge commit**: preserves true history and branch topology; history can get noisy with many small merges
- **Rebase and fast-forward**: linear history that reads like a story and makes `git bisect` and `git log` simpler; rewrites commits
- **Squash merge**: the whole PR becomes one commit on main; clean main history, but you lose the individual commits and the branch cannot be cleanly merged again

A common setup: developers rebase their own branches onto main to stay current, and PRs land with squash or rebase merges for a linear main. Teams that value an audit trail of features choose merge commits. Consistency matters more than the choice.

code.source:
# squash locally (GitHub's "Squash and merge" does the same)
git switch main
git merge --squash feature/search
git commit -m "feat(search): add fuzzy search"

# prefer linear pulls
git config --global pull.rebase true

lesson.heading: Resolving conflicts
lesson.body:
A conflict happens when both sides changed the same lines (or one side edited a file the other deleted) since the merge base. Git stops, writes conflict markers into the file and lists it as unmerged in `git status`.

The process:

- Read `git status` to see which files conflict and whether you are mid-merge or mid-rebase
- Open each file, understand both intents, and write the correct combined code (often neither side verbatim)
- Remove all markers, run the tests, then `git add` the file
- Continue: `git merge --continue` or `git rebase --continue`
- Bail out anytime with `git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort`

During a rebase, "ours" is the branch you are rebasing onto (main) and "theirs" is your commit being replayed, the opposite of a merge. Enable `merge.conflictStyle=zdiff3` to also see the base version, which makes the intent of each side much clearer.

code.source:
<<<<<<< HEAD
const TIMEOUT = 5000;
||||||| base
const TIMEOUT = 3000;
=======
const TIMEOUT = 3000;
const RETRIES = 3;
>>>>>>> feature/retry

# HEAD raised the timeout, the branch added retries.
# Correct resolution keeps both intents:
const TIMEOUT = 5000;
const RETRIES = 3;

lesson.heading: Tools that make conflicts less painful
lesson.body:
- `git checkout --ours file` or `--theirs file` takes one side wholesale (remember the inversion during rebase)
- `git mergetool` opens a configured visual merge tool; VS Code has a built-in 3-way merge editor
- `git rerere` (reuse recorded resolution), enabled with `git config --global rerere.enabled true`, remembers how you resolved a conflict and reapplies it automatically when the same conflict appears again, which helps with repeated rebases
- `git log --merge -p` shows the commits on both sides that touched the conflicting files
- `git diff` during a conflict shows a combined diff of the unresolved parts

Prevention beats tools: small PRs, frequent integration, and separating mass reformatting (like a Prettier run) into its own commit merged quickly.

code.source:
git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3
git config --global rerere.enabled true
git status                      # list unmerged paths
git checkout --theirs package-lock.json && npm install && git add package-lock.json
git rebase --continue

keyPoints: Merge combines histories via the merge base; it fast-forwards when possible and never rewrites commits.
Rebase replays your commits onto a new base, creating new commits with new hashes.
Never rebase commits that others have already pulled and built on.
Squash merge turns a PR into one commit on main; rebase merge keeps commits but linearizes them.
Resolve conflicts by understanding both intents, then `git add` and `--continue`, or `--abort` to start over.
During a rebase, ours/theirs are inverted compared with a merge.
zdiff3 conflict style and rerere make conflicts easier to understand and repeat.

questions.prompt: main has no new commits since feature branched off. What does `git merge feature` on main do by default?
questions.explanation: When the current branch is an ancestor of the merged branch, Git just moves the pointer. Use `--no-ff` if you want a merge commit anyway.

questions.prompt: After `git rebase main` on a feature branch with 3 commits, what is true about those 3 commits?
options: They are replaced by 3 new commits with new hashes
questions.explanation: Rebase creates new commits because the parent pointer changes, and a commit's hash covers its parent. The originals stay reachable in the reflog for a while.

questions.prompt: During `git rebase main`, you run `git checkout --ours app.ts`. Whose version do you get?
options: main's version (the base you are rebasing onto)
questions.explanation: Rebase works by checking out main and applying your commits onto it, so HEAD (ours) is the upstream side and theirs is the commit being replayed. This is the reverse of a merge.

questions.prompt: Which statement about squash merging a PR is correct?
options: It keeps every commit but rewrites messages
It lands the whole PR as a single new commit on the target branch
It creates a merge commit with two parents
It requires a force push to main
questions.explanation: Squash merge applies the combined diff as one new commit with a single parent. The branch's individual commits are not part of main's history.

questions.prompt: You are halfway through a messy rebase and want to return to exactly where you started. What do you run?
questions.explanation: `--abort` restores the branch to its pre-rebase state. `--skip` drops the current commit, which loses work.

questions.prompt: What does enabling `rerere` do?
options: Records conflict resolutions and reapplies them when the same conflict reappears
questions.explanation: rerere stands for reuse recorded resolution. It is useful when you rebase the same branch repeatedly or test-merge long-running branches.

questions.prompt: Merging main into your feature branch rewrites the commits already on the feature branch.
questions.explanation: Merge only adds a new merge commit; existing commits are untouched. That is why merging is safe on shared branches.

questions.prompt: A merge conflict can occur even if the two branches changed different files.
questions.explanation: Most conflicts are overlapping line edits, but a modify/delete or rename conflict (one side edits a file the other deleted or renamed) also stops the merge. Separate files with unrelated edits merge cleanly.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are good reasons to prefer rebasing a personal feature branch onto main before opening a PR?
options: Linear history that is easier to read and bisect
It is the only way to resolve conflicts
Reviewers see your commits on top of current main
It preserves the original commit hashes
It avoids noisy merge commits from main into the branch
questions.explanation: Rebase gives a linear history based on the latest main. Conflicts can be resolved during merges too, and rebase changes hashes rather than preserving them.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: `git merge ___` refuses to create a merge commit and fails unless the merge can fast-forward.
questions.explanation: `--ff-only` guarantees you never create an accidental merge commit; setting `pull.ff=only` applies it to every pull.

questions.prompt: Merge vs rebase: explain the difference and when you would use each.
questions.answer: Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in history. Merge finds the common ancestor and creates a merge commit with two parents (or fast-forwards), preserving exactly what happened and never rewriting commits, so it is safe on shared branches. Rebase replays my commits on top of another branch, creating new commits and a linear history, which is easier to read, review and bisect. The rule is never to rebase commits other people have based work on, because it forces them to reconcile duplicated history. In practice I rebase my own feature branch onto main to stay current and clean up commits before review, and merge (or squash/rebase-merge via the PR tool) into main according to team convention.

questions.prompt: Walk me through how you resolve a nasty merge conflict.
questions.answer:
- Check `git status` to see the conflicting files and whether I am in a merge or rebase.
- Understand intent before editing: `git log --merge -p file` or the PR descriptions tell me why each side changed the code. The zdiff3 style shows the base, so I can see what each side changed.
- Write a resolution that preserves both intents, which is often neither side verbatim. For generated files like lockfiles I take one side and regenerate (`npm install`).
- Remove all markers, build and run the tests before `git add` and `--continue`.
- If it gets confusing, `--abort` and retry, or talk to the author of the other change.
- Afterwards, reduce future conflicts with smaller PRs and more frequent integration.

questions.prompt: A teammate rebased the shared `develop` branch and force pushed. Now your pull shows many duplicate commits. What happened and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: The rebase replaced develop's commits with new copies with different hashes. My local develop still has the old ones, so a normal pull merges old and new versions, duplicating them. If I have no local work on develop, I fetch and run `git reset --hard origin/develop`. If I have local commits on top of the old develop, I use `git rebase --onto origin/develop <old-develop-tip> my-branch` (or a plain `git pull --rebase`, which uses the fork point to skip already-upstream commits) to move only my commits onto the new history. Then I would raise it with the team: protect shared branches against force pushes and keep rebasing to personal branches.

chapters.title: Rewriting History: Interactive Rebase, Reset, Revert and Cherry-pick
chapters.summary: Clean up commits before review, undo changes safely on shared branches, and move individual commits between branches.

lesson.heading: Interactive rebase
lesson.body:
`git rebase -i <base>` opens a todo list of the commits after `<base>`, oldest first. You edit the action word in front of each commit and save:

- `pick` keep the commit
- `reword` keep it but edit the message
- `edit` stop after applying it so you can amend or split it
- `squash` combine with the previous commit and merge the messages
- `fixup` combine with the previous commit and discard this message
- `drop` remove the commit
- reorder lines to reorder commits

This is how you turn "wip", "fix typo", "address review" into a few meaningful commits before merging. Use it on your own branch before others depend on it, then push with `--force-with-lease`.

code.source:
$ git rebase -i origin/main

pick 1a2b3c4 feat: add search endpoint
fixup 5d6e7f8 fix typo
pick 9a8b7c6 feat: add search UI
squash 3c2b1a0 address review comments
drop 7f7f7f7 debug logging

# save and close; Git replays the commits with your instructions

lesson.heading: Fixup commits and autosquash
lesson.body:
When a review comment needs a change to an earlier commit, create a fixup commit that targets it, and let Git place it automatically:

- `git commit --fixup=<sha>` creates a commit titled `fixup! <original subject>`
- `git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main` moves each fixup right after its target and marks it `fixup`
- `git config --global rebase.autoSquash true` makes this the default

To split a commit: mark it `edit`, then when the rebase stops run `git reset HEAD~` (the changes return to the working tree unstaged), stage and commit the pieces separately and `git rebase --continue`.

code.source:
git log --oneline -3
# 9a8b7c6 feat: add search UI
# 1a2b3c4 feat: add search endpoint

# reviewer found a bug in the endpoint commit
git add src/search.ts
git commit --fixup=1a2b3c4
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main
git push --force-with-lease

lesson.heading: Reset: moving the branch pointer
lesson.body:
`git reset <commit>` moves the current branch pointer to `<commit>`. The mode decides what happens to the index and working tree:

- `--soft` moves the branch only; the undone commits' changes stay staged. Great for squashing the last N commits into one.
- `--mixed` (default) moves the branch and resets the index; the changes remain in the working tree, unstaged.
- `--hard` moves the branch and overwrites index and working tree. Uncommitted changes are lost for good; committed ones are recoverable from the reflog.

Reset rewrites the branch, so it is for local or personal history. `git reset --hard origin/main` is the standard way to make a local branch exactly match the remote.

code.source:
git reset --soft HEAD~3        # squash last 3 commits:
git commit -m "feat: add search"

git reset HEAD~1               # undo last commit, keep changes unstaged
git reset --hard origin/main   # discard everything, match remote

lesson.heading: Revert: undoing on shared branches
lesson.body:
`git revert <commit>` creates a **new** commit that applies the inverse of the given commit. History is not rewritten, so it is the correct way to undo something already on main or deployed.

- Revert a range: `git revert A..B` creates one revert per commit (add `--no-commit` to combine them)
- Revert a merge commit: you must choose which parent is the mainline, usually `-m 1` (the branch that was merged into)
- Gotcha: after reverting a merge, merging the same branch again will not bring those changes back, because Git sees them as already merged. To re-land, revert the revert.

In an incident, revert first and fix forward later: it is fast, reviewable and safe.

code.source:
git revert 4f5e6d7                # undo one commit with a new commit
git revert -m 1 8a9b0c1           # undo a merged PR (merge commit)
git revert --no-commit HEAD~3..HEAD && git commit -m "Revert search feature"

lesson.heading: Cherry-pick
lesson.body:
`git cherry-pick <sha>` applies the change introduced by one commit onto the current branch as a new commit. Typical uses:

- backport a fix from main to a release branch (`release/2.3`)
- rescue one good commit from an abandoned branch

Use `-x` to append "(cherry picked from commit ...)" to the message so the link is traceable. Conflicts are resolved like any other, then `git cherry-pick --continue`. Overusing cherry-pick between long-lived branches creates duplicate commits with different hashes and makes later merges confusing; prefer merging the fix forward when branches will be merged anyway.

code.source:
git switch release/2.3
git cherry-pick -x 4f5e6d7         # backport hotfix
git cherry-pick A^..C               # range A through C inclusive
git cherry-pick --abort             # give up on a conflicted pick

keyPoints: Interactive rebase can reorder, reword, squash, fixup, edit and drop commits on your own branch.
`commit --fixup` plus `rebase -i --autosquash` is the cleanest way to address review comments on earlier commits.
reset --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed keeps them unstaged, --hard discards them.
revert creates a new inverse commit and is the safe way to undo shared or deployed history.
Reverting a merge needs `-m 1`; re-landing that branch later requires reverting the revert.
cherry-pick copies one commit's change as a new commit; use -x for traceability when backporting.
After rewriting a pushed personal branch, push with --force-with-lease.

questions.prompt: A bad commit is already on main and deployed. What is the safest way to undo it?
options: Delete the main branch and recreate it
questions.explanation: revert adds a new commit that undoes the change without rewriting history, so nobody's clone breaks and the undo itself is reviewable.

questions.prompt: Which reset mode moves the branch back but leaves the undone changes staged?
questions.explanation: --soft only moves the branch pointer, so the index still holds the content of the old tip and everything appears staged.

questions.prompt: In an interactive rebase todo list, which command merges a commit into the previous one and discards its message?
questions.explanation: fixup combines the change into the previous commit and keeps only the previous commit's message. squash combines and lets you edit the merged messages.

questions.prompt: You need a hotfix that is already on main in the release/2.3 branch. Which command fits?
questions.explanation: Merging main would bring every unreleased feature into the release branch. cherry-pick copies only the fix, and -x records where it came from.

questions.prompt: You reverted a merged PR on main. Later the bug is fixed on the same branch and you merge it again, but the original changes are missing. Why?
options: Git considers the original commits already merged, and the revert commit still undoes them
questions.explanation: The original commits are ancestors of main, so merging only brings in new commits. Revert the revert commit first to bring the original changes back, then merge the fix.

questions.prompt: What does `git commit --fixup=abc123` produce?
options: A new commit titled 'fixup! <subject of abc123>'
questions.explanation: The fixup commit is a normal commit with a special subject. `git rebase -i --autosquash` then moves it after abc123 and marks it as fixup.

questions.prompt: `git reset --hard` can permanently lose uncommitted changes.
questions.explanation: Uncommitted edits are not stored in any commit, so after --hard overwrites the working tree there is nothing in the reflog to recover them from. Committed work is recoverable.

questions.prompt: `git revert` removes the target commit from the branch's history.
questions.explanation: The original commit remains in history; revert adds a new commit containing the inverse change.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which commands rewrite existing commits on the current branch?
options: git reset --soft HEAD~2 followed by a commit
questions.explanation: amend, interactive rebase and reset-then-commit replace existing commits. revert and cherry-pick only add new commits on top.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: to revert a merge commit you must pass ___ 1 to choose the mainline parent.
questions.explanation: A merge commit has two parents, so Git needs to know which side to keep. Parent 1 is the branch that was merged into, usually main.

questions.prompt: Explain git reset --soft, --mixed and --hard, and give a use case for each.
questions.answer: All three move the current branch pointer to the given commit; they differ in what they do to the index and working tree. --soft touches neither, so the changes from the undone commits appear staged; I use it to squash my last few commits into one with `reset --soft HEAD~3` and a new commit. --mixed, the default, also resets the index but leaves files alone, so changes are unstaged; useful to undo a commit and re-stage it differently, or to split a commit during an interactive rebase. --hard resets index and working tree to match the commit; I use it to throw away experiments or match the remote with `reset --hard origin/main`. Uncommitted work is unrecoverable after --hard, but committed work can still be found with the reflog.

questions.prompt: Revert vs reset: when do you use which?
questions.answer: reset rewrites history by moving the branch pointer backwards, so it is only appropriate for commits that have not been shared, or a personal branch where a force push is acceptable. revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous one, leaving history intact, so it is the right tool for main, release branches and anything deployed. Revert is also auditable: the log shows what was undone and why. A special case is merge commits: revert needs `-m 1`, and re-landing the branch later requires reverting the revert. During an incident I revert the offending PR immediately, then fix forward in a normal PR.

questions.prompt: Your PR has 14 commits like 'wip', 'fix', 'oops'. The reviewer asks you to clean it up. How?
questions.answer: I run `git fetch` and `git rebase -i origin/main` to see only my commits. Then I reorder lines to group related changes, mark noise commits as fixup into the commit they belong to, reword messages to explain why, and drop debugging commits. If one commit mixes unrelated work I mark it edit, `git reset HEAD~` and recommit it in pieces with `git add -p`. I run the tests at the end (or `git rebase -i --exec 'npm test'` to test every commit) and push with `--force-with-lease`. Going forward I use `commit --fixup` with autosquash during review so cleanup is automatic. If the team squash-merges anyway, I just make sure the PR title and description are good.

chapters.title: Shell Power Tools: Permissions, Processes, Env Vars, SSH and npm Scripts
chapters.summary: Read and change file permissions, manage processes and ports, configure environment variables, use SSH keys and write reliable npm scripts.

lesson.heading: File permissions and ownership
lesson.body:
`ls -l` shows a permission string like `-rwxr-xr--`. The first character is the type (`-` file, `d` directory, `l` symlink), then three triplets for **user** (owner), **group** and **others**. Each triplet is read (r=4), write (w=2) and execute (x=1).

- `chmod 755 deploy.sh` means rwx for the owner, r-x for group and others: typical for scripts and directories
- `chmod 644 config.json` means rw for the owner, read-only for the rest: typical for files
- `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519` means only the owner can read or write; SSH refuses private keys with looser permissions
- `chmod +x script.sh` adds execute for everyone
- `chown user:group file` changes ownership (usually needs sudo)

On a directory, x means you can enter it and r means you can list it. Avoid `chmod 777`: it lets any user modify the file, which is a security hole, and it usually hides the real ownership problem.

code.source:
ls -l deploy.sh
# -rw-r--r-- 1 ana staff 512 Mar 3 deploy.sh
chmod +x deploy.sh && ./deploy.sh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/app

# script needs a shebang to run directly
head -1 deploy.sh   # #!/usr/bin/env bash

lesson.heading: Processes, signals and ports
lesson.body:
Every running program is a process with a PID. Tools to inspect and control them:

- `ps aux | grep node` lists processes; `top` or `htop` shows live CPU and memory
- `kill <pid>` sends SIGTERM (15): a polite request to shut down, which a server can catch to finish requests and close connections
- `kill -9 <pid>` sends SIGKILL: the kernel ends the process immediately with no cleanup; use only when SIGTERM fails
- Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to the foreground process; Ctrl+Z suspends it, `bg` resumes it in the background, `fg` brings it back
- `cmd &` starts in the background; `nohup cmd &` keeps it running after you log out

"Port 3000 already in use" is common: find the owner with `lsof -i :3000` (macOS/Linux) or `ss -ltnp` (Linux), then kill that PID.

code.source:
lsof -i :3000                # who is listening on 3000
kill 48213                   # SIGTERM, graceful
kill -9 48213                # SIGKILL, last resort
npx kill-port 3000           # cross-platform helper

# Node: handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown (containers send it)
# process.on('SIGTERM', () => server.close(() => process.exit(0)));

lesson.heading: Environment variables and PATH
lesson.body:
Environment variables are key-value strings a process inherits from its parent. They configure programs without code changes (12-factor style): `NODE_ENV`, `DATABASE_URL`, `PORT`.

- `export NAME=value` sets a variable for the current shell and its children; without `export` it is a shell-only variable
- `NAME=value cmd` sets it for one command only
- `env` or `printenv` lists the environment; `echo $NAME` prints one
- Child processes cannot change their parent's environment, which is why a script that exports variables needs to be sourced: `source ./env.sh`
- Persist settings in `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`

`PATH` is a colon-separated list of directories searched for commands. `which node` or `command -v node` shows which binary wins. npm scripts prepend `node_modules/.bin` to PATH, which is why you can run `vitest` in a script without a global install.

In Node, `.env` files are loaded by libraries such as dotenv, or natively with `node --env-file=.env app.js` (Node 20.6+).

code.source:
export DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/app
NODE_ENV=production node server.js     # one-off
echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n'               # one dir per line
command -v node                         # /usr/local/bin/node
node --env-file=.env server.js

lesson.heading: SSH keys and remote access
lesson.body:
SSH authenticates with a key pair: the private key stays on your machine, the public key is added to the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` or to GitHub/GitLab.

- Generate a modern key: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"`, protected with a passphrase
- `ssh-agent` holds the decrypted key so you type the passphrase once per session
- `ssh -T git@github.com` tests GitHub authentication
- `~/.ssh/config` defines host aliases, users, keys and jump hosts
- `scp` and `rsync -avz` copy files over SSH; `ssh -L 5433:localhost:5432 bastion` forwards a local port to a remote database

Never share or commit a private key. The first connection to a host asks you to verify its fingerprint; a later "REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED" warning can mean a rebuilt server or a man-in-the-middle, so verify before removing the old entry.

code.source:
# ~/.ssh/config
Host github.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  AddKeysToAgent yes

Host prod-db
  HostName 10.0.3.15
  User deploy
  ProxyJump bastion.example.com

# usage
# ssh prod-db
# ssh -L 5433:localhost:5432 prod-db   # then connect to localhost:5433

lesson.heading: npm scripts as the project's command line
lesson.body:
The `scripts` field in package.json is the team's shared set of commands. `npm run <name>` executes the script in a shell with `node_modules/.bin` on PATH.

- `pre<name>` and `post<name>` scripts run automatically before and after `<name>`
- `npm test`, `npm start` work without `run`
- Pass extra arguments after `--`: `npm test -- --watch`
- `&&` runs sequentially and stops on failure; for parallel tasks use a tool like `concurrently` or `npm-run-all2`, because `&` behaves differently across shells and Windows
- `npx <pkg>` runs a package binary without installing it globally
- `npm ci` installs exactly what the lockfile says and deletes node_modules first: use it in CI

Keep scripts cross-platform: `rm -rf` and `VAR=x cmd` do not work in Windows cmd, so use packages like `rimraf` and `cross-env` or Node scripts.

keyPoints: Permissions are r=4, w=2, x=1 for user, group and others; 755 for scripts and dirs, 644 for files, 600 for private keys.
SIGTERM allows graceful shutdown; SIGKILL (-9) cannot be caught and skips cleanup.
`lsof -i :PORT` finds the process holding a port.
Exported env vars are inherited by child processes; children cannot modify the parent's environment.
PATH decides which binary runs; npm scripts add node_modules/.bin to it.
Use ed25519 SSH keys with a passphrase and ssh-agent; configure hosts in ~/.ssh/config.
Use `npm ci` in CI, pass extra args with `--`, and keep scripts cross-platform.

questions.prompt: What permissions does `chmod 640 secrets.txt` grant?
options: Owner rw, group r, others none
Owner rwx, group r, others none
Owner r, group rw, others none
questions.explanation: 6 = 4+2 (rw) for the owner, 4 (r) for the group and 0 for others.

questions.prompt: A Node server is stuck on port 3000. Which command first identifies the process?
questions.explanation: lsof -i :3000 lists processes with open sockets on that port, including the PID. `kill -9 3000` would target PID 3000, not port 3000.

questions.prompt: Why should a server process handle SIGTERM?
options: To finish in-flight requests and close connections before exiting
Because SIGKILL calls the SIGTERM handler
questions.explanation: Docker, Kubernetes and process managers send SIGTERM first and wait a grace period before SIGKILL. Handling it enables graceful shutdown without dropped requests.

questions.prompt: You run `./setenv.sh`, which contains `export API_URL=...`. Afterwards `echo $API_URL` prints nothing. Why?
options: The script ran in a child process whose environment is discarded when it exits
questions.explanation: Executing a script starts a new shell. Use `source ./setenv.sh` (or `. ./setenv.sh`) to run it in the current shell.

questions.prompt: How do you pass `--watch` to the command behind `npm test`?
questions.explanation: Arguments after `--` are forwarded to the script's command. Without it, npm treats `--watch` as its own config flag.

questions.prompt: SSH refuses to use your private key with the message 'UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE'. What fixes it?
questions.explanation: SSH requires private keys to be readable only by the owner. 600 gives the owner read/write and nobody else access.

questions.prompt: A process can catch and handle SIGKILL to run cleanup code.
questions.explanation: SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked or ignored. The kernel terminates the process immediately, which is why it is the last resort.

questions.prompt: Inside an npm script you can call binaries from local devDependencies (such as eslint) without npx or a global install.
questions.explanation: npm prepends node_modules/.bin to PATH when running scripts, so locally installed binaries resolve directly.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which practices are correct for CI pipelines in Node projects?
options: Use npm ci instead of npm install
Chain checks with && so the job fails on the first error
questions.explanation: npm ci with a committed lockfile gives reproducible installs and && propagates failures. Secrets belong in the CI secret store, and 777 permissions are never the right fix.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: `ssh-keygen -t ___` generates a modern elliptic-curve key that is recommended over RSA.
questions.explanation: Ed25519 keys are short, fast and secure, and are supported by GitHub, GitLab and current OpenSSH.

questions.prompt: How do environment variables work, and how should an application manage configuration and secrets across environments?
questions.answer: Environment variables are key-value strings in a process's environment, inherited by child processes at start; a child cannot change its parent's environment. Following 12-factor, the same build artifact runs everywhere and reads config (database URL, API base URL, feature flags) from the environment. Locally I use a git-ignored `.env` and commit a `.env.example` documenting required keys. In CI and production, values come from the platform's secret store (GitHub Actions secrets, Vercel or AWS Secrets Manager), never from the repo. I validate config at startup (for example with zod) so a missing variable fails fast. In frontend frameworks, only explicitly public prefixed variables (like `NEXT_PUBLIC_`) are inlined into the client bundle, so secrets must never use that prefix.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGKILL, and how you would implement graceful shutdown in a Node service.
questions.answer: SIGINT is what Ctrl+C sends to the foreground process. SIGTERM is the standard termination request sent by `kill`, Docker and Kubernetes. Both can be caught. SIGKILL cannot be caught: the kernel stops the process immediately, with no cleanup. For graceful shutdown I register `process.on('SIGTERM', ...)` that stops accepting new connections with `server.close()`, lets in-flight requests finish, closes database pools and queue consumers, then exits with 0. I add a timeout that forces exit before the orchestrator's grace period (30 seconds by default in Kubernetes) runs out, and in Kubernetes I fail the readiness probe first so the load balancer stops routing traffic.

questions.prompt: A deploy script works on your Mac but fails in CI with 'Permission denied'. How do you debug it?
questions.answer:
- Check the execute bit: `ls -l deploy.sh`. Git tracks the executable flag, so if it was committed without +x, CI checks it out non-executable. Fix with `git update-index --chmod=+x deploy.sh` or `chmod +x` and commit (on Windows the first is needed).
- Check the shebang line exists and points to an available interpreter (`#!/usr/bin/env bash`); CI images might lack bash.
- Check line endings: CRLF from Windows editors makes `/usr/bin/env bash\r` fail; `.gitattributes` with `*.sh text eol=lf` fixes it.
- Check which user CI runs as and the ownership of target directories.
- Reproduce locally in the same container image to confirm.
