chapters.title: Team Workflows, Conventional Commits and Code Review
chapters.summary: Compare trunk-based development and GitFlow, write Conventional Commits, and run pull requests and code reviews that keep quality high without slowing the team.

lesson.heading: Trunk-based development
lesson.body:
In trunk-based development everyone integrates small changes into one main branch (the trunk) at least daily. Feature branches, if used, live for hours or a couple of days.

- Incomplete features ship dark behind **feature flags**, so merging is decoupled from releasing
- CI runs on every PR and on main; main must always be releasable
- Releases are cut from main, often continuously deployed
- Merge conflicts stay small because nobody diverges for long

The DORA research (Accelerate, State of DevOps reports) associates trunk-based development with higher deployment frequency and lower change failure rates. It requires good automated tests and the discipline to split work into small, safe increments.

lesson.heading: GitFlow and release branches
lesson.body:
GitFlow (Vincent Driessen, 2010) uses long-lived `main` and `develop` branches plus `feature/*`, `release/*` and `hotfix/*` branches. Features merge into develop; a release branch stabilizes a version and merges into both main (tagged) and develop; hotfixes branch from main.

It fits software with explicit versioned releases and several supported versions in the field: mobile apps, desktop software, on-premise products, libraries. For continuously deployed web apps it adds overhead and long-lived divergence; Driessen himself later noted it is not the best fit for continuous delivery.

Middle grounds are common: **GitHub flow** (branch from main, open PR, merge, deploy) and trunk-based with short-lived **release branches** for backporting fixes to a shipped version.

code.source:
GitFlow
  main      o-----------o---------o   (tags: v1.0, v1.1)
  hotfix         \--h--/|
  release           r---r
  develop   o--o--o--o--o--o
  feature    \-f-f-/

GitHub flow
  main      o----o----o----o   (deploy after each merge)
  feature    \-a-b-/ \-c-/

lesson.heading: Conventional Commits and semantic versioning
lesson.body:
Conventional Commits is a spec for commit messages: `type(scope)!: description`, optional body and footers.

- `feat:` a new feature (maps to a MINOR version bump)
- `fix:` a bug fix (PATCH)
- `feat!:` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer signals a breaking change (MAJOR)
- Other common types: `docs`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`, `style`

Because messages are machine-readable, tools like semantic-release, release-please and changesets can bump versions and generate changelogs automatically. commitlint with a commit-msg hook (via husky or lefthook) enforces the format. Teams that squash-merge often only enforce the format on PR titles, since the title becomes the commit on main.

code.source:
feat(auth): add passkey login

Users can register a passkey from account settings.
Falls back to password login on unsupported browsers.

Closes #482

---
fix(cart): prevent negative quantities

refactor(api)!: rename /users/:id/profile to /profiles/:id

BREAKING CHANGE: the old route returns 410 Gone.

lesson.heading: Writing pull requests that get reviewed fast
lesson.body:
The biggest lever for review speed is **size**. Small PRs (a few hundred lines at most) get faster and more thorough reviews; large ones get skimmed.

A good PR:

- does one thing; refactors and behavior changes go in separate PRs
- has a title that states the outcome and a description covering why, what changed, how it was tested, and screenshots or recordings for UI
- links the ticket and calls out risky areas or open questions for the reviewer
- passes CI before requesting review; use draft PRs to share early work
- is self-reviewed first: read your own diff in the PR UI, which catches leftover logs and typos

Stacked PRs (a chain of small dependent PRs) let you keep moving while earlier parts are reviewed.

code.source:
## Why
Checkout fails for carts with >50 items (timeout in tax service).

## What
- Batch tax lookups in groups of 20
- Add retry with backoff on 503

## How tested
- Unit tests for batching edge cases (0, 1, 20, 21, 51 items)
- Manually checked out a 120-item cart on staging

## Risk
Tax service rate limit: 100 req/s. Batching reduces calls 20x.

lesson.heading: Giving good code reviews
lesson.body:
Code review exists to catch defects, share knowledge and keep the codebase consistent. Google's engineering practices put it simply: approve once the change improves the overall code health, even if it is not perfect.

- Review in priority order: correctness and security, design and architecture, tests, readability, then style (which should be automated by linters and formatters)
- Respond within one business day; slow reviews are a major source of lost throughput
- Comment on the code, not the person; ask questions ("what happens if items is empty?")
- Label severity: prefix optional comments with `nit:` and separate blocking issues clearly
- Explain why and suggest alternatives, using suggestion blocks where possible
- Praise good solutions too

As an author, do not take comments personally, reply to every comment, and move long debates to a quick call, then record the outcome in the PR.

code.source:
Blocking: this query runs inside the loop, so a 100-item order
makes 100 DB calls. Could we fetch all products with one
WHERE id IN (...) before the loop?

nit: `data` -> `invoices` would make the intent clearer.

Question: is it intentional that admins skip the rate limit?

Nice: the table-driven tests make the edge cases very clear.

keyPoints: Trunk-based development: small changes merged to main daily, feature flags for unfinished work, main always releasable.
GitFlow suits versioned releases with multiple supported versions; it is heavy for continuously deployed apps.
Conventional Commits (feat, fix, feat!/BREAKING CHANGE) map to semver bumps and enable automated changelogs.
PR size is the main driver of review speed and quality.
A PR description covers why, what, how it was tested, and risks.
Review for correctness, design and tests first; automate style with linters and formatters.
Approve when the change improves code health; label nits as non-blocking.

questions.prompt: With Conventional Commits and semantic-release, which commit triggers a MAJOR version bump?
questions.explanation: The `!` after the type (or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer) marks a breaking change, which maps to MAJOR. feat maps to MINOR and fix to PATCH.

questions.prompt: In trunk-based development, how do teams merge unfinished features without exposing them to users?
questions.explanation: Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature, so code can merge to main continuously while staying hidden.

questions.prompt: Which project is the best fit for GitFlow?
options: A SaaS web app deployed 20 times a day
A desktop app that supports v3 and v4 in parallel with scheduled releases
questions.explanation: GitFlow's release and hotfix branches model explicit versions and maintenance of shipped releases. Continuous deployment works better with trunk-based or GitHub flow.

questions.prompt: Which change most improves the speed and quality of code review?
questions.explanation: Reviewers can reason about a small diff completely and quickly. Large diffs get superficial reviews and wait longer in the queue.

questions.prompt: A team squash-merges every PR. Where is the most useful place to enforce Conventional Commits?
options: Every commit on the feature branch
The PR title, which becomes the squash commit message
questions.explanation: Only the squash commit lands on main, and its message defaults to the PR title. Linting PR titles gives the changelog tooling what it needs without policing work-in-progress commits.

questions.prompt: What should a reviewer focus on first?
options: Whether the author used their preferred library
questions.explanation: Defects and design problems are expensive later; style should be enforced by tools. Spending review time on nits while missing a bug is the common failure.

questions.prompt: In trunk-based development, main should be kept in a releasable state at all times.
questions.explanation: Because everyone integrates into main constantly and releases are cut from it, a broken main blocks the whole team. CI gates and fast reverts protect it.

questions.prompt: A good reviewer withholds approval until the code matches exactly how they would have written it.
questions.explanation: The standard is whether the change improves overall code health. Personal preference is not a reason to block; mark such comments as nits or optional.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: what belongs in a strong PR description?
options: Screenshots or recordings for UI changes
Known risks or areas needing careful review
questions.explanation: The description gives context the diff cannot: motivation, verification, visuals and risk. The diff is already in the PR.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: in Conventional Commits, a footer starting with ___ signals a breaking change.
questions.explanation: The spec accepts `BREAKING CHANGE:` (or the synonym `BREAKING-CHANGE:`) in the footer, or `!` after the type/scope.

questions.prompt: Compare trunk-based development and GitFlow. Which would you choose for a new web product?
questions.answer: GitFlow has long-lived main and develop branches plus feature, release and hotfix branches. It suits products with explicit versions and multiple maintained releases, but branches diverge for longer and merges get bigger. Trunk-based development has everyone merging small changes into main at least daily, with feature flags hiding unfinished work and main always releasable. For a continuously deployed web product I would choose trunk-based (or GitHub flow with short-lived branches): faster feedback, smaller conflicts, and research like DORA links it to better delivery performance. It requires investment in CI, automated tests and a feature flag system. If we later had to support shipped versions, I would add short-lived release branches with cherry-picked fixes rather than adopting full GitFlow.

questions.prompt: How do you give feedback in code review, especially to a more senior engineer or on a contentious change?
questions.answer: I focus on the code and its effects, not the person, and phrase concerns as questions or observations with reasons: "If two requests hit this at once, could we double-charge? A unique constraint on order_id would prevent it." I separate blocking issues from nits explicitly. Seniority does not change the bar: senior engineers make mistakes too, and most appreciate a well-reasoned catch. If a thread goes back and forth more than twice I suggest a short call, then summarize the decision in the PR so the reasoning is recorded. When there is a real design disagreement that should have been settled before coding, I propose a short design doc or bring in a tech lead rather than blocking indefinitely.

questions.prompt: Your team's PRs wait two to three days for review. How would you fix it?
questions.answer:
- Measure first: time to first review, PR size and review rounds, from the Git host's data.
- Make PRs smaller: set an expectation (for example under 400 changed lines), use stacked PRs and feature flags.
- Set a team norm: first response within one business day, and reviews take priority over starting new work, since unmerged code delivers no value.
- Automate the trivial: formatters, linters, type checks and tests in CI so humans do not comment on style.
- Use CODEOWNERS and auto-assignment so each PR has a clear reviewer instead of a diffusion of responsibility.
- Revisit in a retro after a few weeks with the metrics.

chapters.title: Git Internals: Objects, Trees, Commits and Refs
chapters.summary: Learn how Git stores blobs, trees, commits and tags in a content-addressed object database, and how refs, HEAD and packfiles fit together.

lesson.heading: A content-addressed object database
lesson.body:
Under the porcelain commands, Git is a key-value store. Every piece of content is stored as an object whose key is the hash of its type, size and content. The same content always produces the same hash, so identical files are stored once, and any corruption is detectable because the hash would no longer match.

There are four object types:

- **blob**: the content of a file (no file name, no permissions)
- **tree**: a directory listing; each entry has a mode, a name and the hash of a blob or subtree
- **commit**: a pointer to one root tree, zero or more parent commits, author, committer and message
- **tag**: an annotated tag object pointing to another object, with tagger and message

Objects live in `.git/objects`, either as individual zlib-compressed files (loose objects) or inside packfiles.

code.source:
echo 'hello' | git hash-object --stdin
# ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a  (same on every machine)

git cat-file -t HEAD          # commit
git cat-file -p HEAD          # tree, parent, author, committer, message
git cat-file -p 'HEAD^{tree}' # entries: mode, type, hash, name
git count-objects -vH         # loose vs packed size

lesson.heading: How a commit is built
lesson.body:
When you run `git commit`, Git writes a tree object for each directory from the index (reusing existing trees and blobs whose hashes did not change), then a commit object pointing at the root tree and the current HEAD commit as parent, and finally moves the current branch ref to the new commit's hash.

Because a commit includes its parent's hash, and the parent includes its own parent's, each commit hash cryptographically covers the entire history before it. Change one old commit and every descendant's hash changes, which is exactly what you see after a rebase.

A merge commit simply has two (or more) parents. A root commit has none. Renames are not stored: Git detects them heuristically when diffing by comparing content similarity.

code.source:
$ git cat-file -p HEAD
tree 9c1f0a...
parent 3b18e5...
author Ana Lima <ana@example.com> 1767225600 +0000
committer Ana Lima <ana@example.com> 1767225600 +0000

feat: add search

$ git cat-file -p 9c1f0a
100644 blob a1b2c3...    package.json
040000 tree d4e5f6...    src
100755 blob 0f9e8d...    deploy.sh

lesson.heading: Refs, HEAD and the reflog
lesson.body:
Refs are human-readable names for hashes, stored as files under `.git/refs` or in `.git/packed-refs` (newer Git versions can also use the reftable format):

- `refs/heads/main` local branches
- `refs/remotes/origin/main` remote-tracking branches
- `refs/tags/v1.0.0` tags

`.git/HEAD` normally contains a symbolic ref like `ref: refs/heads/main`; in detached state it contains a hash.

The **reflog** records every position each ref and HEAD has held locally: commits, checkouts, resets, rebases, merges. It is local only (never pushed) and entries expire, by default 90 days for reachable entries and 30 days for unreachable ones. This is your safety net: commits are rarely truly lost while they are in the reflog.

code.source:
cat .git/HEAD                  # ref: refs/heads/main
git rev-parse main             # resolve a ref to a hash
git show-ref --heads --tags
git reflog -10                 # HEAD's history
git reflog show feature/login
# a1b2c3d HEAD@{0}: rebase (finish): returning to refs/heads/feature/login
# 9f8e7d6 HEAD@{5}: commit: add validation

lesson.heading: Revision syntax
lesson.body:
Many commands accept revision expressions:

- `HEAD~3` third ancestor following first parents; `HEAD^2` the second parent of a merge commit
- `main@{yesterday}`, `HEAD@{2}` reflog-based positions
- `A..B` commits reachable from B but not A ("what is on B that A lacks")
- `A...B` symmetric difference: commits on either side but not both; in `git diff A...B` it means diff from the merge base to B, which is what a PR shows
- `:/fix login` the most recent commit whose message matches
- `HEAD:src/app.ts` a file's content at a commit

`git rev-parse` resolves any of these to a hash, which is handy in scripts.

code.source:
git log --oneline main..feature     # what the PR adds
git diff main...feature             # PR-style diff from merge base
git show HEAD~2:package.json        # file as it was 2 commits ago
git log -1 HEAD^2                   # second parent of a merge
git rev-parse --short HEAD          # 7a3f9c1

lesson.heading: Packfiles, garbage collection and large repos
lesson.body:
Loose objects are periodically compressed into **packfiles**, which store many objects with delta compression between similar versions. `git gc` (run automatically from time to time) packs objects and prunes unreachable ones that are older than the expiry window.

An object is unreachable when no ref, reflog entry or index entry points to it, directly or through ancestry. That is why a commit lost during a bad reset survives until its reflog entry expires and gc prunes it.

For very large repositories:

- `git clone --depth 1` shallow clone (only recent history, common in CI)
- `git clone --filter=blob:none` partial clone that fetches file contents on demand
- `git sparse-checkout` checks out only some directories of a monorepo
- Git LFS stores large binaries outside the object database, keeping pointer files in the repo
- `git maintenance start` schedules background tasks such as commit-graph updates and prefetching

code.source:
git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/org/monorepo.git
cd monorepo
git sparse-checkout set apps/web packages/ui

git gc --prune=now      # pack and prune now (careful: drops recoverable garbage)
git fsck --lost-found   # list dangling commits and blobs

keyPoints: Git stores four object types: blob (content), tree (directory), commit (tree + parents + metadata) and tag.
Objects are addressed by the hash of their content, so identical content is stored once and corruption is detectable.
A commit's hash covers its parents, so changing history changes every descendant hash.
Branches and tags are refs pointing to hashes; HEAD points to a ref or directly to a commit.
The reflog is a local log of where refs have been and is the main tool for recovering lost commits.
`A..B` lists commits on B not on A; `git diff A...B` diffs from the merge base, like a PR.
Packfiles, gc, shallow/partial clones and sparse-checkout keep large repositories manageable.

questions.prompt: Which Git object stores a file's name?
options: None, names are stored in refs
questions.explanation: A blob holds only content. The tree that contains it maps the name and mode to the blob's hash, which is why renaming a file creates a new tree but reuses the blob.

questions.prompt: Two developers on different machines commit a file with identical content. What is true about the blob hashes?
questions.explanation: A blob hash depends only on type, size and content. Commits differ (author, time, parent), but the blob is the same object.

questions.prompt: Why does editing the message of a commit 10 commits back change the hashes of the 9 newer commits?
options: Each commit's content includes its parent's hash
Git re-hashes the whole repository on every change
questions.explanation: The edited commit gets a new hash, so its child's parent field changes, giving the child a new hash, and so on up the chain.

questions.prompt: What does `.git/HEAD` usually contain when you are on the main branch?
options: The hash of the latest commit
The tree of the working directory
questions.explanation: HEAD is a symbolic ref to the current branch. Only in detached HEAD state does it contain a raw hash.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the diff a GitHub PR from feature into main displays?
questions.explanation: Three dots in git diff compares the merge base of main and feature with feature, showing only the branch's changes, not changes made on main since branching.

questions.prompt: What does `git clone --filter=blob:none` do?
options: Clones commits and trees but downloads file contents on demand
questions.explanation: A blobless partial clone keeps full history metadata (useful for log and blame) but fetches blobs lazily when checked out or needed.

questions.prompt: The reflog is pushed to the remote so teammates can recover your lost commits.
questions.explanation: The reflog is strictly local to each repository. A commit that only existed in your clone and was lost is only recoverable from your reflog.

questions.prompt: Git explicitly records file renames inside commit objects.
questions.explanation: Commits store snapshots only. Rename detection happens at diff or log time by comparing content similarity (for example `git log --follow`).

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are Git object types?
questions.explanation: Branches are refs (files containing a hash), not objects. Annotated tags are real objects; lightweight tags are just refs.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: `git cat-file ___ HEAD` pretty-prints the content of the commit object.
questions.explanation: `-p` pretty-prints any object; `-t` prints its type and `-s` its size.

questions.prompt: Explain how Git stores data internally. What happens when you run git commit?
questions.answer: Git is a content-addressed object store. Blobs hold file contents, trees hold directory listings mapping names and modes to blob or tree hashes, commits point to a root tree plus parent commits and metadata, and annotated tags point to other objects. Every object's ID is the hash of its content. On `git commit`, Git turns the index into tree objects (reusing unchanged blobs and subtrees by hash), writes a commit object with the root tree, the current HEAD commit as parent, author, committer and message, then updates the current branch ref to the new hash and logs it in the reflog. Because parents are part of the hash, a commit ID identifies the whole history behind it. Branches are just refs, which is why branching is cheap.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a branch, a tag and HEAD at the implementation level?
questions.answer: All three are refs. A branch is a file under refs/heads containing a commit hash, and Git moves it automatically when you commit while it is checked out. A tag under refs/tags also holds a hash but never moves; a lightweight tag points straight at a commit, while an annotated tag points at a tag object containing the tagger, date, message and an optional signature. HEAD is a special symbolic ref naming the current branch (`ref: refs/heads/main`), or containing a raw hash when detached. Commands like commit, reset and merge work by updating whichever branch HEAD points to.

questions.prompt: Your monorepo takes 15 minutes to clone in CI and gigabytes on laptops. What Git features would you use?
questions.answer:
- In CI, use shallow clones (`--depth 1`, the default in actions/checkout) unless the job needs history, such as changelog generation or affected-project detection, in which case fetch just enough depth or use a blobless clone.
- On laptops, use partial clone (`--filter=blob:none`) plus sparse-checkout so developers only materialize the directories they work on.
- Move large binaries (design files, test fixtures, videos) to Git LFS or out of the repo; check history for big blobs with `git rev-list --objects --all` and `git cat-file --batch-check`, and rewrite history with git filter-repo if needed, coordinated with the team.
- Enable `git maintenance` (commit-graph, prefetch) and fsmonitor for faster status.
- Cache dependencies separately in CI rather than committing them.

chapters.title: Recovery and Debugging: Reflog, Bisect, Blame, Worktrees and Hooks
chapters.summary: Recover lost commits and branches, find the commit that introduced a bug with bisect, trace code history, and automate checks with hooks.

lesson.heading: Recovering lost work with the reflog
lesson.body:
Almost every "I lost my work" situation involving committed changes is recoverable, because Git does not delete commits immediately; it only moves refs. The reflog shows where HEAD and each branch pointed before.

- After a bad `reset --hard`: `git reflog`, find the entry before the reset, `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` (or the hash)
- After a botched rebase: find `rebase (start)` in the reflog and reset to the entry just before it, or use `ORIG_HEAD`, which rebase, merge and reset set to the previous tip
- Deleted branch: find its last commit in the reflog and `git branch name <hash>`
- Dropped stash: `git fsck --unreachable | grep commit` lists candidates; stash commits have messages like "WIP on main"

What cannot be recovered: changes that were never committed or staged. Staged-but-uncommitted content exists as blobs and can sometimes be found with `git fsck --lost-found`, but without file names.

code.source:
git reset --hard HEAD~3          # oops
git reflog
# 1f2e3d4 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
# 9a8b7c6 HEAD@{1}: commit: add payment webhook
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}        # back where we were

git branch -D feature/x          # oops
git reflog | grep feature/x
git branch feature/x 5c6d7e8     # recreated

lesson.heading: Finding the culprit with git bisect
lesson.body:
`git bisect` performs a binary search through history to find the first bad commit. With 1,000 commits between a known good and known bad version, it needs about 10 tests (log2 of 1000).

- `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad` (current commit), `git bisect good v2.1.0`
- Git checks out a midpoint; test it and mark `good` or `bad`
- Repeat until Git prints "<hash> is the first bad commit"
- `git bisect skip` if a commit cannot be tested (for example it does not build)
- `git bisect reset` returns to where you started

Automate it with `git bisect run <script>`: the script exits 0 for good, 1-127 (except 125) for bad, and 125 for skip. A failing test written for the bug makes a perfect bisect script. Bisect works best when every commit builds and passes tests, another reason for atomic commits and squash/rebase discipline.

code.source:
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v2.1.0
# Bisecting: 312 revisions left to test after this (roughly 8 steps)

git bisect run npx vitest run src/cart/total.test.ts
# 4e5f6a7 is the first bad commit
git bisect reset

lesson.heading: Tracing history: blame, log -L and pickaxe
lesson.body:
When code looks wrong, find out why it was written that way before changing it.

- `git blame file` shows the last commit that touched each line; `-w` ignores whitespace changes and `-C` detects lines moved or copied from other files
- `.git-blame-ignore-revs` lists bulk formatting commits to skip; configure it with `git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs` (GitHub honors it automatically)
- `git log -L 40,60:src/cart.ts` shows the evolution of a line range; `git log -L :calculateTotal:src/cart.ts` follows a function
- `git log -S 'discountRate'` finds commits that added or removed a string; `-G 'regex'` matches changed lines by regex
- `git log --follow file` continues history across renames

Blame points to a commit; the commit message, PR and linked ticket explain the why. This is why good commit messages pay off.

code.source:
git blame -w -C -L 40,60 src/cart.ts
git log -L :calculateTotal:src/cart.ts
git log -S 'discountRate' --oneline
git log --follow --oneline -- src/utils/money.ts
echo 3f4a5b6c... >> .git-blame-ignore-revs   # prettier mass reformat

lesson.heading: Worktrees and stash for context switching
lesson.body:
`git worktree` checks out another branch into a separate directory that shares the same repository. You can review a PR or fix a production bug without stashing or disturbing your current work, and both checkouts share objects, so it is cheap.

- `git worktree add ../hotfix release/2.3`
- `git worktree list`, `git worktree remove ../hotfix`
- A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time

`git stash` remains handy for quick switches: `stash push -m msg -- path` stashes specific paths, `-u` includes untracked files, `stash apply` keeps the entry while `pop` drops it, and `stash branch name` creates a branch from a stash when it no longer applies cleanly.

code.source:
git worktree add ../app-hotfix -b hotfix/login origin/main
cd ../app-hotfix && npm ci && npm test
# ...fix, commit, push...
cd - && git worktree remove ../app-hotfix

git stash push -u -m "half-done refactor"
git stash list
git stash branch refactor-wip stash@{0}

lesson.heading: Hooks and automated guardrails
lesson.body:
Git hooks are scripts in `.git/hooks` that run on events: `pre-commit`, `commit-msg`, `pre-push`, `post-checkout`, and on servers `pre-receive`. Because `.git/hooks` is not versioned, teams share hooks with tools like **husky** or **lefthook**, or with `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`.

Good uses:

- `pre-commit`: lint and format only the staged files (lint-staged), scan for secrets
- `commit-msg`: validate Conventional Commits with commitlint
- `pre-push`: run fast unit tests or type checks

Keep hooks fast (a few seconds) or developers will bypass them with `--no-verify`. Client-side hooks are a convenience, not enforcement: anyone can skip them, so the real gate is CI plus branch protection (required status checks, required reviews, no force pushes on main).

keyPoints: Committed work is almost always recoverable via the reflog or ORIG_HEAD until gc prunes it.
Uncommitted, unstaged changes are not stored by Git and cannot be recovered after reset --hard or restore.
git bisect binary-searches history; `bisect run` automates it with a test script (exit 0 good, 125 skip, other non-zero bad).
blame -w -C, log -L, log -S and --follow explain why code looks the way it does.
.git-blame-ignore-revs hides mass formatting commits from blame.
Worktrees give extra checkouts sharing one repository, ideal for hotfixes and reviews.
Client-side hooks (husky, lefthook) are convenience; CI and branch protection are the real enforcement.

questions.prompt: You ran `git reset --hard HEAD~2` and lost two commits. What is the fastest recovery?
options: git reflog, then git reset --hard to the entry before the reset
questions.explanation: The reflog lists the previous HEAD position (often HEAD@{1}). Resetting back to it restores the branch with both commits.

questions.prompt: About how many test steps does git bisect need to search 1,000 commits?
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the range each step; log2(1000) is just under 10.

questions.prompt: In `git bisect run ./check.sh`, what should the script exit with when the current commit cannot be tested?
questions.explanation: 125 tells bisect to skip the commit. 0 means good, other codes from 1 to 127 mean bad, and values above 127 abort the bisect.

questions.prompt: A mass Prettier reformat makes `git blame` useless. What is the standard fix?
options: Rewrite history to remove the formatting commit
List the commit in .git-blame-ignore-revs and configure blame.ignoreRevsFile
questions.explanation: Blame skips the listed commits and attributes lines to the previous meaningful change. GitHub's blame view reads the file automatically.

questions.prompt: You are mid-way through a big change and need to fix a production bug on another branch without touching your working directory. Which feature fits best?
questions.explanation: A worktree creates a second checkout of another branch in a different folder, sharing the same object database, so your current files are untouched.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the history of a single function across commits?
questions.explanation: `git log -L` with the `:funcname:file` form tracks the line range of that function through history and prints each change.

questions.prompt: A pre-commit hook installed with husky guarantees that no unlinted code reaches main.
questions.explanation: Developers can bypass hooks with --no-verify, or never install them. Enforcement must happen in CI with required status checks on protected branches.

questions.prompt: After a rebase, ORIG_HEAD points to the branch tip as it was before the rebase.
questions.explanation: Rebase, merge and reset record the previous tip in ORIG_HEAD, so `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` undoes the operation (until another such command overwrites it).

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which situations can usually be recovered with Git alone?
options: A branch deleted with git branch -D yesterday
Commits lost after a bad interactive rebase
Edits never staged, discarded with git restore
A file you deleted that was never added to Git
questions.explanation: Deleted branches and rewritten commits are in the reflog, and dropped stash commits are dangling objects findable with fsck. Content Git never stored cannot be recovered by Git.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: `git bisect ___ npm test` automatically runs the test command at each step.
questions.explanation: `bisect run` uses the command's exit code to mark each commit good, bad or skip until it finds the first bad commit.

questions.prompt: A regression appeared somewhere in the last 400 commits and nobody knows where. How do you find it?
questions.answer: I use git bisect. First I write the smallest reliable reproduction, ideally a failing automated test or script that exits non-zero when the bug is present. Then `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad HEAD`, `git bisect good <last known good tag>`. With `git bisect run ./repro.sh` Git binary-searches automatically, about 9 steps for 400 commits. Commits that do not build exit 125 to be skipped. When it reports the first bad commit, I read its diff and PR to understand the cause, run `git bisect reset`, and fix with a regression test. If the history has many broken intermediate commits, bisect gets noisy, which is an argument for atomic commits that each pass CI.

questions.prompt: A junior engineer says they force pushed and 'lost a week of work'. How do you help?
questions.answer:
- Stay calm and stop further damage: no more gc, resets or pushes until we look.
- If the work was committed on their machine, their local reflog has it: `git reflog show feature-branch` or `git reflog`, find the last good commit, and create a branch at it.
- If they overwrote the remote with an older local copy, anyone who fetched recently has the old commits as `origin/branch` in their clone. GitHub's PR timeline also shows force-pushed commit hashes, and those commits often stay fetchable for a while.
- Restore with `git push --force-with-lease` from the recovered branch.
- Then prevent it: explain `--force-with-lease`, protect shared branches, and push work daily.

questions.prompt: How would you set up Git hooks for a team, and what belongs in hooks versus CI?
questions.answer: I would version the hooks with husky or lefthook so they install automatically on `npm install`. pre-commit runs lint-staged (ESLint and Prettier on staged files only) and a secret scanner like gitleaks; commit-msg runs commitlint if we use Conventional Commits; pre-push might run type checks or affected unit tests. Hooks must stay fast, a few seconds, or people bypass them with --no-verify. Since hooks are optional and local, everything important is repeated in CI: full lint, type check, tests, build, security scans, with required status checks and reviews on protected branches. Hooks give fast feedback; CI is the gate.
